items.abstract: <jats:p>Cancer drug resistance is increasingly understood to be mediated by long non-coding RNA (lncRNA) and microRNA (miRNA) regulatory networks, yet computational models typically treat lncRNA-drug and miRNA-drug resistance as separate, static prediction tasks. This paper proposes a Dose-Aware Heterogeneous Graph Transformer (HGT) that jointly models lncRNA, miRNA, and drug entities as a single heterogeneous graph, extending meta-relation-typed attention with a dose-conditioned gating mechanism and a cross-layer attention pooling module for interpretability. Because no real dataset was available in this working environment, the architecture is validated as a proof-of-concept (PoC) on a synthetic heterogeneous graph, implemented and trained from scratch in numpy (no GPU deep-learning framework was available), with manual backpropagation verified against numerical gradients. Two implementations are compared: a fixed-projection encoder with a trained prediction head, and a fully end-to-end trainable encoder. Both recover above-chance predictive signal (AUC 0.52-0.60), but a 5-seed replication with paired significance testing finds no statistically detectable benefit from dose-conditioning (p = 0.895) or cross-layer attention (p = 0.635) at this scale, a properly tested null result rather than an unresolved limitation. We report these results transparently, situate them against the closest published models (iNcRD-HG; MHGTMDA) via a qualitative comparative-positioning table, and specify the real-data validation required before the architecture's specific contributions can be properly evaluated.</jats:p>
title: A Heterogeneous Graph Transformer with Dose-Aware Cross-Layer Attention for Joint lncRNA-miRNA-Drug Resistance Association Prediction in Cancer

items.abstract: <jats:p>Acquired drug resistance in cancer develops progressively rather than instantaneously, with regulatory rewiring of lncRNA-miRNA competing-endogenous-RNA networks occurring over the course of treatment rather than as a single static event. Existing computational models of this process either model temporal dynamics without an explicit, mechanistically-motivated lncRNA-miRNA cross-attention structure (the closest prior work uses a hierarchical graph autoencoder with LSTM-based dose conditioning), or model lncRNA-miRNA regulatory interactions without any temporal dimension. This paper proposes a Cross-Attention Transformer that models regulatory interaction between lncRNA and miRNA expression at each timestep via cross-attention, and models how this regulatory axis evolves via causal temporal self-attention across timesteps, to predict eventual resistance phenotype from an observed trajectory. Because no real time-course single-cell dataset was available in this working environment, the architecture is implemented and evaluated as a proof-of-concept (PoC) on a synthetic trajectory dataset modeling ceRNA-style coevolution, using hand-derived backpropagation verified against numerical gradients (no GPU deep-learning framework was installable in this sandboxed environment). A 5-seed replication with paired significance testing finds no statistically detectable benefit from either the cross-attention mechanism (p = 0.345) or the temporal self-attention mechanism (p = 0.503) individually, extending a pattern observed across two companion proof-of-concept papers in this research program in which specific attention/gating mechanisms have not yet shown robust ablation benefits at small synthetic scale. A genuinely informative finding, independent of the ablation result, is that the full model's ability to predict eventual resistance is near chance using only the first third of the observed trajectory and reaches its performance plateau only once roughly five of six timesteps are observed, a concrete, testable characterization of how much temporal observation this task requires. We report all results transparently and specify the real time-course data needed to properly validate the architecture.</jats:p>
title: A Cross-Attention Transformer for Temporal Modeling of lncRNA-miRNA Regulatory Axis Dynamics During Single-Cell Drug Resistance Evolution

items.abstract: <jats:p>Antiretroviral drug resistance is a persistent problem in achieving sustained viral suppression in diverse populations, and is a driver of HIV treatment failure. Current predictive models tend to categorize patients as responders or non-responders, an outcome that is too vague for clinicians to make meaningful decisions about treatment. In this paper we introduce ViralGuide, a tri-modal ensemble framework that independently estimates the probability of resistance to each of the four drug classes of interest (NRTIs, NNRTIs, Protease Inhibitors, INSTIs) via a combined processing of HIV genomic sequence in a Bidirectional LSTM network and structured Drug Resistance Mutation flags with normalized clinical parameters in gradient-boosted classifiers. Monte Carlo Dropout inference is used to estimate uncertainty and ensemble outputs are fed into a WHO guideline-aligned recommendation engine which outputs specific ART regimens with traceable clinical reasoning. Interpretability is tackled at the patient level through waterfall plots of SHAP values and counterfactual explanations of modifiable clinical features and longitudinal trajectory modelling over treatment visits. The findings reflect that the system can successfully improve discrimination rates per class as compared to the single-modality baseline systems, which make it a viable tool for linking resistance prediction to individual treatment planning for HIV treatment. In addition, the system enriches the predictions with clinically meaningful context features such as the level of HIV disease (based on CD4 levels) and an estimate of HIV subtype (based on the mutation pattern). These additions add to the interpretability and provide greater clinical context for decision-making.</jats:p>
title: Viralguide: Drug-Class-Level HIV Resistance Prediction using Bidirectional LSTM, Xgboost Ensemble and Cross-Modal Attention Fusion

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                <jats:p>Accurate prediction of drug-target affinity (DTA) is a core challenge in computational drug discovery. Structure-based methods depend on experimentally determined protein coordinates, which are unavailable for most drug-relevant targets. sequence-only approaches, in turn, operate on linear residue representations and lack an explicit mechanism to encode the spatial proximity relationships that govern protein-ligand interactions. We present XAttn-DTA, a sequence-driven framework that addresses both limitations without requiring experimental structural data. Drug molecules are encoded as 2D molecular graphs via multilayer Graph Attention Networks (GATs), capturing atomic topology and bond-level chemistry. Proteins are represented as residue-level graphs constructed from ESM2-predicted contact maps, that captures inter-residue coevolutionary and structural signals embedded within the sequence. The bidirectional cross-attention fusion module projects both embeddings into a shared latent space and applies dual multi-head cross-attention. This enables ligand and protein residue environments to inform one another. On the Davis benchmark, XAttn-DTA achieves a concordance index (CI) of 0.907 and MSE of 0.175, improving CI by 1.8% and reducing MSE by 9.3% over the strongest baseline. On KIBA, it achieves an MSE of 0.121, a 13.6% reduction. Under three strict cold-start settings across Davis, KIBA, and BindingDB, the model yields MSE reductions of up to 79.0% and CI improvements of up to 31.5% over the strongest baseline, demonstrating strong generalization to unseen scaffolds and novel protein families.</jats:p>
title: Sequence-Driven Drug-Target Affinity Prediction Via Graph Attention Networks and Bidirectional Cross-Attention Fusion

items.abstract: Drug--target interaction (DTI) prediction plays a critical role in virtual screening and computational drug discovery. Existing Transformer-based models such as MolTrans improve sequence representation learning but still rely on implicit interaction modelling, limited global semantic aggregation, and optimisation strategies that are sensitive to dataset imbalance and scarce-data settings. In this work, we propose a strengthened Transformer-based DTI framework integrating three key components: a bidirectional cross-attention mechanism for explicit modelling of drug--protein dependencies, a hybrid local--global representation scheme combining CNN-based interaction modelling with multi-scale global pooling, and a residual-enhanced classification head with stabilised optimisation using BCEWithLogitsLoss, AdamW, and cosine learning-rate scheduling. Comprehensive experiments on the BindingDB, BIOSNAP, and DAVIS benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed framework consistently outperforms MolTrans across multiple evaluation metrics, achieving up to 2.4 percentage-point improvements in AUROC and 11.8 percentage-point improvements in AUPRC. The largest gains are observed on the small and imbalanced DAVIS dataset, indicating improved robustness under scarce-data conditions. Ablation studies further confirm that cross-attention and global semantic aggregation contribute complementary performance benefits. Overall, the proposed framework provides a more expressive, interpretable, and robust approach for DTI prediction under realistic drug discovery settings.
title: Bidirectional Cross-Attention and Global Semantic Aggregation for Robust Drug–Target Interaction Prediction

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Motivation</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Accurate prediction of HIV drug resistance from viral sequences is critical for optimizing antiretroviral therapy. Traditional machine-learning approaches using binary mutation encoding achieve strong accuracy but may fail to capture epistatic interactions and structural features relevant to resistance mechanisms. Protein language models (PLMs) offer learned representations encoding evolutionary and structural information, but have not been systematically benchmarked for HIV resistance prediction across the modern antiretroviral drug set.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We evaluated ESM-2 (650 M parameters) with attention-weighted pooling for predicting resistance to 18 drugs across three classes (protease inhibitors, NRTIs, NNRTIs) on the Stanford HIVDB dataset (n = 6308 sequences). Attention-weighted ESM-2 embeddings significantly outperformed XGBoost baselines with binary mutation encoding (mean AUC 0.968 versus 0.955, P = .0017), with gains across 15 of 18 drugs and the largest improvements for drugs with complex resistance patterns. Attention weights showed 2.48-fold enrichment at known drug-resistance-mutation positions (P &lt; .05 for 63% of drugs; NRTIs strongest at 4.20-fold). External validation on a 20% holdout showed minimal degradation (AUC 0.934). Benchmarking against ESM C 600M and ESM-1v confirmed performance is robust to PLM choice (mean AUC 0.942–0.946 across backbones). Performance was maintained across HIV-1 subtypes (B 0.924; B-divergent 0.900; non-B 0.884) and a temporal holdout (AUC 0.930).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Availability and implementation</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Source code is available at https://github.com/hayden-farquhar/HIV-ESM-2 under an MIT license and archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19466629. Stanford HIVDB genotype–phenotype data are publicly available at https://hivdb.stanford.edu/.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Protein language model embeddings improve HIV drug resistance prediction: a comprehensive benchmark with attention-based interpretability

items.abstract: Despite significant progress in existing methods for predicting drug-target binding affinity, there is still room for improvement in better utilizing molecular sequences and designing feature fusion strategies. Addressing these two points, we propose a novel computational model, Secondary Sequence and Cross-attention Block based Drug-Target binding Affinity prediction (SSCBDTA). The model is composed of sequence encoding, feature extraction, modal fusion and a decoder, with three innovations: (i) applying the byte pair encoding algorithm to process vast unlabeled data for obtaining molecular secondary sequences; (ii) extracting features from two perspectives: the primary and secondary sequences of molecules; (iii) combining cross-attention and criss-cross attention to fuse the extracted features of drugs and proteins. In two benchmark datasets, SSCBDTA outperforms ten state-of-the-art models on nearly all evaluation metrics. By conducting four different ablation experiments, we separately validated the effectiveness of molecular secondary sequences and multiple cross-attention in improving the prediction accuracy and stability of SSCBDTA. We also utilized SSCBDTA to predict binding affinities between 3,137 FDA-approved drugs and 6 SARS-CoV-2 replication-related proteins, identifying a number of promising molecules that could be further developed as anti-COVID drugs.
title: SSCBDTA: Prediction of Drug-Target Binding Affinity with Secondary Sequences and Multiple Cross-Attention Blocks
